chapters.name: Chapter 1: The license and the core ideas

lessons.title: Lesson 1: How a real estate license works in your state
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List your state's steps to a salesperson license from the official page.
This lesson builds toward: Using your state real estate regulator's official website, you will list the steps to a salesperson license in the right order, with no step missing and the official page named.
There is no national real estate license in the US. Each state has its own regulator, often called a real estate commission or department of real estate. It decides the classes, the exam, the background check and the fees. ARELLO, the association of license law officials, keeps a list of regulators you can use to find yours.
The steps are similar in most states: meet the age rule, finish state-approved pre-license classes, apply, pass a background check (often fingerprints), pass the exam, and work under a licensed broker. Many exams have a national part and a state law part.
The details differ a lot. California asks for three college-level courses (Real Estate Principles, Real Estate Practice and one elective). Texas asks for 180 classroom hours in six courses, fingerprints with the state police, and exams given by Pearson. Your state may be different, so always read your own state's page.
Step by step:
- Find your state's real estate regulator (use the ARELLO list or search your state name plus "real estate commission" and look for .gov).
- Open the page for a new salesperson or sales agent license.
- Write each step in order: age, classes, application, background check, exam, broker.
- Write down the page address and the date you checked it.
Words to know:
- Real estate regulator: the state office that licenses agents and enforces the rules, such as a real estate commission.
- Salesperson (sales agent): the first real estate license; you work under a broker.
- Broker: a higher license; a broker can run a real estate office and supervise salespeople.
- Pre-license education: the state-approved classes you must finish before the exam or the license.
- Sponsoring broker: the broker who agrees to supervise you once you are licensed.
Official sources:
- ARELLO (Association of Real Estate License Law Officials): Regulatory agencies
- California Department of Real Estate: Salesperson license requirements
- Texas Real Estate Commission: Become a sales agent
Try it now: Find your state's real estate regulator. On paper, list every step to a salesperson license in order, with the page address and today's date. Circle any step you did not know about.
You can now find your state's real estate regulator and list the steps to a salesperson license in order.

check.q: Who decides the classes and exam for a real estate salesperson license?
options: The real estate company you join
The bank that lends to buyers
check.why: Real estate licenses are issued by each state, and the state regulator sets the requirements.

check.q: A website you found says the classes take 60 hours. What do you do?
options: Check the hours on your state regulator's official page
Trust it if it looks professional
Pay for the cheapest class now
Ask a friend in another state
check.why: Hours differ by state and change, so only your state's official page is reliable.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Property and ownership words the exam uses
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Identify the correct term for a property or ownership situation.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short description of a property or ownership situation, you will identify the correct real estate term for it, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Real property is the land and everything attached to it, such as a house, a fence or a tree, plus the rights that come with it. Personal property is movable, such as a couch. A fixture was personal property but is now attached, like a ceiling fan or a built-in dishwasher, so it usually goes with the house.
Owning real property means holding a bundle of rights: to possess, use, enjoy, exclude others and sell or pass it on. Fee simple is the most complete form of ownership. When two or more people own together, joint tenancy usually includes the right of survivorship (a share passes to the other owners at death), while tenancy in common does not.
A deed transfers ownership; title is the right of ownership itself. Things that limit or burden a property are encumbrances: a lien (a money claim, such as a mortgage or unpaid tax) and an easement (a right to use someone else's land, such as a utility line). Land is described in three main ways: metes and bounds, the rectangular (government) survey system, and lot and block from a recorded map.
Words to know:
- Real property: land, what is attached to it, and the rights of ownership.
- Fixture: an item attached to the property, so it is treated as part of it.
- Fee simple: the most complete form of ownership.
- Right of survivorship: when one co-owner dies, their share passes to the other co-owners.
- Encumbrance: anything that limits or burdens a property, such as a lien or an easement.
- Lien: a legal money claim on a property.
- Easement: a right to use part of someone else's land for a set purpose.
Try it now: Make 10 flash cards on paper: the term on the front and your own plain meaning plus one example on the back (real property, personal property, fixture, fee simple, joint tenancy, tenancy in common, deed, title, lien, easement). Quiz yourself twice.
You can now name the right real estate term for common property and ownership situations.

check.q: The power company has the right to run a line across the back of a yard. This is:
check.why: An easement is a right to use part of someone else's land for a set purpose.

check.q: Two sisters own a house. When one dies, her share passes to the other automatically. They most likely hold title as:
check.why: Joint tenancy usually includes the right of survivorship; tenancy in common does not.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Agency duties and fair housing
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose the action that follows agency duties and fair housing law in a scenario.
This lesson builds toward: Given a scenario with a client or a home seeker, you will choose the action that follows agency duties and fair housing law, getting at least 4 of 5 scenarios right and naming the rule.
When you represent a client, you are their agent and owe them fiduciary duties. Many textbooks list them as OLDCAR: Obedience (to lawful instructions), Loyalty, Disclosure (of important facts), Confidentiality, Accounting (for money held) and Reasonable care. Your state's law sets the exact duties and the disclosure forms.
Representing both buyer and seller in one deal is called dual agency. Some states allow it only with written consent from both sides, and some limit or ban it. Check your state's rules.
The federal Fair Housing Act makes it illegal to discriminate in housing because of race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status (such as having children) or disability. States and cities may add more groups. Illegal practices include steering (guiding people toward or away from areas because of a protected class), blockbusting (pushing owners to sell by warning that a group is moving in) and redlining (refusing loans or insurance in certain areas).
Step by step:
- Ask: who is my client, and what do I owe them?
- Ask: does this request treat someone differently because of a protected class?
- If yes, do not do it; explain the law politely.
- Write down what happened and tell your broker.
Words to know:
- Agent: a person authorized to act for someone else (the client or principal).
- Fiduciary: a person in a position of trust who must put the client's interests first.
- Dual agency: one agent or brokerage representing both buyer and seller in the same deal.
- Protected class: a group the law protects from discrimination, such as race or disability.
- Steering: guiding people toward or away from areas because of a protected class; illegal.
Official sources:
- HUD: Fair Housing Act overview
Try it now: Write three short scenarios where a seller or buyer asks you to do something unfair (for example, "Don't show my house to families with kids"). For each, write the protected class involved and one polite sentence you would say instead.
You can now apply agency duties and fair housing law to choose the right action with clients.

check.q: A seller says, "Only show my house to people without children." What do you do?
options: Explain that familial status is protected and you must show it to everyone
Agree, since the seller is your client
Ask the buyers how many children they have
check.why: Familial status is a protected class under the Fair Housing Act, and obedience covers only lawful instructions.

check.q: Your seller tells you the lowest price they will accept. A buyer asks you for it. Which duty applies?
check.why: An agent keeps the client's private information, such as their lowest price, confidential.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Contracts, math and your test plan

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Contracts and the path to closing
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check a purchase offer for the parts of a valid contract and order the closing steps.
This lesson builds toward: Given a sample purchase offer, you will check that it has the parts of a valid contract and put the closing steps in order, with no missing part and the federal disclosure timing correct.
A valid contract needs: parties who are legally able to sign (competent), an offer and an acceptance (mutual agreement), consideration (something of value given by each side), and a lawful purpose. A contract to buy or sell real estate generally must be in writing to be enforced; this rule is called the statute of frauds.
A contract is void if it was never valid (for example, an illegal purpose). It is voidable if one side may cancel it, for example when a minor signed it. Most purchase offers include contingencies, such as getting a loan or a good inspection, and earnest money, a deposit that shows the buyer is serious.
A common path is: offer, acceptance, escrow or closing agent opened, inspection, appraisal and loan approval, final walk-through, and closing. Federal rules protect the borrower: the lender gives a Loan Estimate within three business days of the loan application, and a Closing Disclosure at least three business days before closing, so the buyer can compare them.
Step by step:
- Check the parties are named and able to sign.
- Check there is a clear offer and a signed acceptance.
- Check the price, the earnest money and what each side gives (consideration).
- Check it is in writing and for a lawful purpose.
- List the contingencies and their deadlines.
- Put the closing steps in order, with the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure timing.
Words to know:
- Consideration: something of value each side gives, such as money or a promise.
- Statute of frauds: the rule that real estate contracts generally must be in writing to be enforced.
- Void / voidable: void: never a valid contract; voidable: valid, but one side may cancel it.
- Contingency: a condition that must happen for the deal to go ahead, such as loan approval.
- Earnest money: a deposit the buyer makes to show they are serious.
- Closing Disclosure: the lender's final form with the loan terms and closing costs.
Official sources:
- CFPB: What is a Loan Estimate?
- CFPB: What is a Closing Disclosure?
- CFPB: Buying a house (Owning a Home)
Try it now: Write a short made-up purchase offer (names, address, price, earnest money, one contingency, signatures). Then check it with the six steps above and list what is missing. Finish with the closing steps in order.
You can now check a purchase offer for the parts of a valid contract and put the steps to closing in order.

check.q: A buyer and seller agree on a house sale by phone only. Under the statute of frauds the deal is:
options: Generally not enforceable until it is in writing
check.why: Real estate contracts generally must be in writing to be enforced.

check.q: When must the borrower get the Closing Disclosure?
options: At least three business days before closing
check.why: The CFPB says the lender gives the Closing Disclosure at least three business days before closing.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Real estate exam math
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate commission, loan-to-value, property tax, proration and area.
This lesson builds toward: Given an exam-style word problem and a calculator, you will calculate commission, loan-to-value, property tax, proration and area, getting at least 4 of 5 right with the work shown.
Practice only: all numbers here are made up. Commission: sale price times the rate. A $300,000 sale at 6% is $18,000. If the listing office gets half, that is $9,000; if the agent's split is 60%, the agent gets $5,400.
Loan-to-value (LTV) is the loan divided by the value. A $240,000 loan on a $300,000 home is 0.80, or 80%. Property tax is the assessed value times the tax rate: $200,000 times 1.5% is $3,000 a year, or $250 a month.
Proration splits a cost by days. If yearly taxes are $3,650 and the year has 365 days, that is $10 a day; if the seller owned the home 120 days and the buyer pays the bill later, the seller owes the buyer $1,200. Area: length times width. A lot 50 feet by 120 feet is 6,000 square feet. One acre is 43,560 square feet. Check whether your exam uses a 360-day or 365-day year.
Step by step:
- Read the question and underline what it asks for.
- Write the formula (part = whole times rate).
- Turn percentages into decimals (6% = 0.06).
- Do one step at a time on paper.
- Ask: does the answer make sense?
Words to know:
- Commission: the fee paid for selling, usually a percentage of the sale price.
- Split: how a commission is shared between offices or between a broker and an agent.
- Loan-to-value (LTV): the loan amount divided by the property value, as a percentage.
- Assessed value: the value the local government uses to figure property tax.
- Proration: dividing a cost between buyer and seller by the days each one owns the property.
Try it now: Practice only. Solve on paper with a calculator: (1) 5% commission on $250,000; (2) LTV of a $180,000 loan on a $200,000 home; (3) yearly tax on a $150,000 assessed value at 2%; (4) seller's share of $1,825 yearly taxes for 73 days (365-day year); (5) square feet in a lot 80 feet by 100 feet. Answers: $12,500; 90%; $3,000; $365; 8,000.
You can now solve the common math on a real estate exam and show your work.

check.q: Practice only: what is the LTV of a $270,000 loan on a $300,000 home?
Practice only: a lot is 100 feet by 150 feet. How many square feet is it?
check.why: Area is length times width: 100 times 150 is 15,000 square feet.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your study and test plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a dated study and test plan from your state's exam content outline.
This lesson builds toward: Using your state's exam content outline and a calendar, you will write a dated study and test plan, covering every outline topic and your three weakest topics. Using your state real estate regulator's official website, you will list the steps to a salesperson license in the right order, with no step missing and the official page named.
Your state or its testing company publishes a candidate handbook. It usually has the exam content outline (the topics and how many questions on each), the rules for test day, the ID you must bring and how to schedule. Download it from the official site, not from a copy someone posted.
Turn the outline into a plan. List every topic, rate yourself 1 to 3 on each, and mark your three weakest. Put the big dates on a calendar working backward from a target exam date: finish classes, apply, get fingerprints, schedule the exam. Then set short study blocks each week, with practice questions and math every week.
Practice tests help most when you review every wrong answer and write why the right answer is right. Beware of any site that promises a "guaranteed pass" or sells real exam questions; that is a scam or cheating, and states can deny a license for it.
Step by step:
- Download your state's candidate handbook from the official site.
- Copy the exam content outline topics.
- Rate yourself 1 to 3 on each topic; mark your three weakest.
- Set a target exam date and work backward to each step.
- Plan weekly study blocks with practice questions and math.
- Review every wrong answer and write why the right answer is right.
Words to know:
- Candidate handbook: the official guide to the exam: topics, rules, ID and scheduling.
- Exam content outline: the list of topics on the exam and how much each counts.
- Target date: the date you aim to take the exam; you plan backward from it.
Official sources:
- ARELLO (Association of Real Estate License Law Officials): Regulatory agencies
- Texas Real Estate Commission: Become a sales agent
- California Department of Real Estate: Salesperson license requirements
Try it now: Final task: make your Real Estate License Study and Test Plan: your state's steps with dates and the official page, the outline topics with your three weakest marked, a rule sheet on agency, fair housing and contracts, five worked math problems, and a weekly schedule up to your exam date.
You can now turn your state's exam outline into a dated study and test plan and follow it.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Official steps Steps are missing, out of order, or copied from an unofficial site. Every step from the state regulator's page is listed in order, with the page address and the date checked. Also notes the costs and documents for each step exactly as the official page states them. Core terms Several property or ownership terms are wrong or missing from the rule sheet. The rule sheet defines the key property and ownership terms correctly in plain words. Each term has a real-life example the learner made up. Agency and fair housing Fiduciary duties or the seven federal protected classes are missing or wrong. Lists the duties and all seven federal classes, plus steering, blockbusting and redlining. Adds any extra protected classes from the learner's state or city, with the source. Contract and closing Contract parts or closing steps are missing, or the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure timing is wrong. Lists every part of a valid contract and the closing steps in order with correct disclosure timing. Adds the contingencies and their deadlines from a sample offer. Math Fewer than 4 of the 5 problems are right, or the work is not shown. At least 4 of 5 problems are right with the work shown. All 5 right, plus one extra problem written and solved by the learner. Dated plan No target date, or topics are not from the official content outline. Covers every outline topic, marks the three weakest and has weekly study blocks up to a target date. Includes practice-test review dates and a backup exam date. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and check it again.

check.q: Where should your study plan's topic list come from?
options: Your state's official exam content outline
A site selling real exam questions
check.why: The official content outline shows what the exam actually tests.

check.q: You keep missing proration questions on practice tests. What is the best plan?
options: Skip proration; it is only a few questions
Mark it as a weak topic and add math practice each week
check.why: Marking weak topics and practicing them every week closes the gap before test day.
